title_en: Chenzhou Damiyin Anti-Counterfeiting Technology Co., Ltd. v. National Intellectual Property Administration — administrative dispute over refusal of trademark registration review
ruling_gist_en: To determine whether a mark for trademark registration has distinctive character, first consider the distinctiveness constituted by its meaning, pronunciation, and appearance — i.e., whether the general public can identify the mark as an indicator of the source of goods or services. Second, in specific circumstances, further consider the cognitive habits of the relevant public in the field of the designated goods or services, as well as the actual usage in the relevant industry, etc., to conduct a specific, comprehensive, and holistic judgment on whether the mark can indicate the source of goods or services.

full_text_en:
【Ruling Gist】

In determining whether a mark for trademark registration has distinctive features, the first consideration should be the identifiability of its own meaning, pronunciation, and appearance—that is, whether the general public can recognize and treat the mark as an indicator of the source of goods or services. Second, under specific circumstances, a concrete, comprehensive, and overall assessment of whether the mark can indicate the source of goods or services shall be made, further integrating the cognitive habits of the relevant public in the field of the designated goods or services, as well as the actual usage in the relevant industry.

Supreme People's Court
Administrative Ruling
(2023) Zui Gao Fa Xing Shen No. 1053

Retrial Applicant (Plaintiff at first instance, Appellant at second instance): Chenzhou Da Mu Yin Anti-Counterfeiting Technology Co., Ltd. Domicile: Room 502, Building 1, No. 54, Guimenling Community, Beihu Street, Beihu District, Chenzhou City, Hunan Province.

Legal Representative: Tang Zhiying, Executive Director of the Company.

Agent ad litem: Liao Zhengliang, lawyer of Hunan Xinghe Law Firm.

Respondent (Defendant at first instance, Appellee at second instance): National Intellectual Property Administration. Domicile: No. 6, Xitucheng Road, Jimenqiao, Haidian District, Beijing.

Legal Representative: Shen Changyu, Director of the Administration.

Agent ad litem: Zhang Ling, Examiner of the Administration.

The Retrial Applicant, Chenzhou Da Mu Yin Anti-Counterfeiting Technology Co., Ltd. (hereinafter referred to as Da Mu Yin Company), applied to this Court for retrial against the administrative judgment (2022) Jing Xing Zhong No. 6436 of the Beijing High People's Court (hereinafter referred to as the judgment of second instance) in the case of administrative dispute over trademark application refusal review with the Respondent, National Intellectual Property Administration. This Court formed a collegial panel to conduct the review, which has now concluded.

Da Mu Yin Company applied for retrial on the following grounds: Viewed as a whole, the trademark No. 52444799, "Da Mu Yin Seller Promises Trademark Fake One Pay Hundred Times and Design" (hereinafter referred to as the trademark in question; see attached figure at the end of the document), has distinctive features and should be approved for registration. (1) The vertically arranged Chinese characters "大拇印" (Da Mu Yin) are located in the center of the trademark in a larger font and constitute the distinctive part of the trademark in question. Da Mu Yin Company has applied for multiple trademarks using the Chinese characters "大拇印", all of which were approved for registration, indicating that the characters "大拇印" have distinctive features. (2) The framed Chinese characters "卖家承诺商标假一赔百" (Seller Promises Trademark Fake One Pay Hundred Times) are located below the vertically arranged "大拇印" characters. The relevant public generally recognizes them as the operator's guarantee of the authenticity of the upper "大拇印" trademark, thereby increasing the overall distinctiveness of the mark. (3) The trademark in question itself has an anti-counterfeiting function, which is a major breakthrough in the trademark field and can promote the development of China's anti-counterfeiting industry. It requests this Court to retry according to law.

The National Intellectual Property Administration submitted its opinion stating that the judgment of second instance had clear facts and correct application of law and should be affirmed.

Upon review, this Court finds that the dispute focus of this retrial review is whether the trademark in question falls under the circumstance of lacking distinctive features.

Article 11, Paragraph 1 of the Trademark Law of the People's Republic of China (hereinafter referred to as the Trademark Law) provides: "The following signs shall not be registered as trademarks: (1) those that consist exclusively of the generic name, design, or model of the goods in respect of which the trademark is used; (2) those that merely directly indicate the quality, principal raw materials, function, intended purpose, weight, quantity, or other characteristics of the goods; and (3) those that are devoid of any distinctive character."

A mark applied for trademark registration must have distinctive features, which is a prerequisite for obtaining trademark registration. A mark with distinctive features should enable the relevant public to recognize and memorize it, so that it can be used to indicate the source of goods or services. This is also the function and value of a trademark. In determining whether a mark for trademark registration has distinctive features, the first consideration should be the identifiability of its own meaning, pronunciation, and appearance—that is, whether the general public can recognize and treat the mark as an indicator of the source of goods or services. Second, under specific circumstances, a concrete, comprehensive, and overall assessment of whether the mark can indicate the source of goods or services shall be made, further integrating the cognitive habits of the relevant public in the field of the designated goods or services, as well as the actual usage in the relevant industry.

First, regarding whether the meaning, pronunciation, and appearance of the trademark in question enable the public to identify or memorize it as a sign indicating the source of goods or services. The trademark in question consists of the larger text "大拇印" (Da Mu Yin) in the upper part and the smaller text "卖家承诺商标假一赔百" (Seller Promises Trademark Fake One Pay Hundred Times) enclosed in a frame in the lower part, both in ordinary printed font. Da Mu Yin Company argues that because the text "大拇印" itself is distinctive, the addition of the text "卖家承诺商标假一赔百" enhances the distinctiveness of the mark. Generally, appending other decorations or words to a registered trademark mark does not necessarily impair its distinctiveness, and may sometimes even increase it. However, some additions may be superfluous and actually diminish the distinctiveness of the original mark. As to the trademark in question, "卖家承诺" (Seller Promises) and "商标假一赔百" (Trademark Fake One Pay Hundred Times) are common advertising slogans used to promise authenticity, and "大拇印" in this context also carries a meaning of promise. Their combination actually dilutes the distinctiveness of "大拇印" when it stands alone. The trademark in question as a whole is easily recognized by the general public as a commonplace advertising slogan making a promise of authenticity, rather than a mark indicating the source of goods or services. Therefore, the trademark in question lacks distinctiveness. Second, Da Mu Yin Company further argues that the relevant public tends to interpret the lower part "卖家承诺商标假一赔百" as the operator's promise of the authenticity of the upper "大拇印" mark. However, a trademark's self-authentication function is not a factor to be considered in determining its distinctiveness. Da Mu Yin Company's claim that the trademark in question is distinctive because it has a self-authentication function cannot be sustained. Finally, Da Mu Yin Company failed to provide evidence to prove that the trademark in question has acquired distinctiveness through use.

In summary, the trademark in question lacks the distinctive features required for trademark registration. The judgment of second instance’s determination that the trademark in question falls under the circumstance specified in Article 11, Paragraph 1, Item (3) of the Trademark Law is not improper.

The retrial application of Da Mu Yin Company does not satisfy the circumstances provided in Article 91 of the Administrative Procedure Law of the People's Republic of China. Pursuant to Article 116, Paragraph 2 of the Interpretation of the Supreme People's Court on the Application of the Administrative Procedure Law of the People's Republic of China, the ruling is as follows:

The retrial application of Chenzhou Da Mu Yin Anti-Counterfeiting Technology Co., Ltd. is dismissed.
